name: Dental work / teeth maxxing

lead: Teeth maxxing means improving how teeth look, mostly by whitening them with strips, pastes, trays or dentist treatments. It is among the more evidence-backed softmaxes.
Randomized trials and reviews show peroxide whitening changes tooth colour. Forum users also discuss DIY methods that have not been studied.

paras: Hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in the tooth. Whitening toothpastes mainly remove surface stains with abrasives.
Tooth sensitivity is frequently reported, and strong peroxide can irritate or burn gums. Regulators limit peroxide strength in retail products; over-abrasive products can damage tooth tissue.

lead: Teeth maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of improving the colour and look of the teeth, most often through whitening. Community discussion centres on whitening strips, toothpastes, dentist treatments and do-it-yourself methods, often alongside orthodontics and other dental work [1][2].

Tooth whitening typically uses hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, which break down pigment molecules [3]. Reviews and trials describe clear colour changes, with tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the most commonly reported side effects, and regulators limit peroxide concentrations in retail products [3][4][5].
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide, carbamide peroxide, abrasive toothpastes
EU retail limit 0.1% H2O2; higher only via dentists

paras: Wikipedia lists in-office gels (about 10-44% carbamide peroxide), tray-based gels worn for hours or overnight, strips and gels applied over about two weeks, rinses, and toothpastes that lighten gradually through abrasives and low peroxide levels [3]. Whitening works best on yellow teeth and least on grey ones, and heavily stained teeth may need bonding or veneers [3]. Teeth maxxing also covers non-whitening dental work such as alignment and veneers, though the main body of forum discussion is about whitening.

A 2023 systematic review examined the prognosis of at-home bleaching with low-concentration products [4]. A randomized trial in adolescents compared hydrogen peroxide products with placebo over a 12-month follow-up, assessing colour change, sensitivity and discomfort [5]. A critical review of modern whitening concepts and a review of natural whitening ingredients are also published [6][7].
Wikipedia notes results can partly relapse as teeth rehydrate after intensive in-office sessions, and a 2015 study found light activation did not improve results [3].

Wikipedia reports sensitivity in 67-78% of in-office patients lasting 4-39 days, with less sensitivity from home use, and says peroxide at 10% or above can burn soft tissue, especially with poorly fitting trays [3]. A review of natural whitening states high-concentration peroxide products can cause demineralisation through oxidation, while natural ingredients lighten teeth without eroding surfaces [7]. Very abrasive toothpastes can harm dental tissue [3].

In the EU, retail whitening products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6% allowed only under a dental professional for patients aged 18 and over; the US FDA endorses gels up to 6% hydrogen peroxide or 16% carbamide peroxide [3]. An editorial in the British Dental Journal addresses illegal teeth whitening [8].

On looksmax.org users ask about whitening strips, coffee staining, tooth sensitivity and cheaper alternatives. In one thread a user reports strips were too painful to keep on for five minutes, and replies suggest coconut oil or a forum member's DIY whitening guide [1]. Other threads discuss whether that DIY procedure worked [9][10]. Dental authorities and the research cited here address professionally supervised methods; they do not evaluate forum DIY protocols.

Randomized trials and systematic reviews of tooth whitening exist [4][5][6]. They evaluate commercial and professional whitening products, not forum DIY protocols; no studies were found of the DIY methods discussed on looksmax.org.
